slides.title: Appendix C: Review of Lie Groups
slides.notes: Open by positioning Appendix C as a working toolkit for the rest of Riemannian geometry. The point is not to memorize a catalog of groups, but to recognize when a geometric construction has smooth multiplication, infinitesimal generators, and an action on a manifold.

slides.title: Reading Map: From Definitions To Actions
slides.notes: Use the dependency map as the lecture route. Start with the smooth group object, pass to its tangent space at the identity, then return to geometry through actions. Emphasize that the notebook turns this reading route into checkable artifacts rather than a list of isolated vocabulary.

slides.title: Lie Group = Smooth Manifold + Group Law
slides.notes: This slide should slow down the two compatibility requirements. Multiplication and inversion are algebraic operations, but the appendix asks them to be smooth maps. That compatibility is exactly why matrix groups, circles, and isometry groups can be studied with differential geometry.

slides.title: Tangent Space At The Identity
slides.notes: Introduce the Lie algebra as the infinitesimal shadow of the group. The tangent space at the identity carries more than linear structure once left-invariant vector fields are identified with tangent vectors. The bracket records the first noncommutative behavior.

slides.title: Exponential Map: Local Motion From Algebra
slides.notes: Explain the exponential map as a bridge, not a magic formula. A tangent vector determines a one-parameter subgroup, and evaluating it at time one returns a nearby group element. For matrices this resembles the usual matrix exponential, but the geometric meaning is broader.

slides.title: Adjoint Action And Bracket
slides.notes: Here the key message is that conjugation differentiates twice: first it gives the adjoint representation on the Lie algebra, and then its derivative gives the bracket. This makes the bracket visible as the infinitesimal change caused by moving one symmetry through another.

slides.title: Group Actions On Manifolds
slides.notes: Group actions are the appendix's return route to Riemannian manifolds. An action assigns a diffeomorphism to each group element, so algebraic composition becomes geometric motion. Orbits, stabilizers, and infinitesimal generators organize how much symmetry a point sees.

slides.title: Invariant Metrics And Curvature Checks
slides.notes: Connect the notebook's local chart and curvature proxy to invariant geometric thinking. A Lie group action can preserve a metric, and invariance turns many local computations into algebraic data. The plotted metric determinant and signed proxy give a concrete inspection target.

slides.title: Common Failure Modes
slides.notes: This warning slide prevents a common overgeneralization. A group is not automatically a Lie group, a smooth action is stronger than a pointwise permutation, and the exponential map need not be globally onto or one-to-one. These distinctions matter in later model-space examples.

slides.title: Takeaways For Riemannian Geometry
slides.notes: Close by tying the appendix to the main course. Lie groups supply examples, Lie algebras supply linearized computations, and actions supply symmetry reductions. The lasting habit is to ask where smooth algebra becomes a geometric invariant that can be checked.
